title: Perfect Number Finder
story: Ancient Greeks were obsessed with perfect numbers — numbers equal to the sum of their proper divisors. 6 = 1+2+3. 28 = 1+2+4+7+14. Only 51 perfect numbers are known. You can find the first four in milliseconds.
why: Finding perfect numbers combines divisor-finding with accumulation — a practical algorithm that teaches systematic search patterns.
analogy: Perfect numbers are like recipes where the ingredients (divisors) add up exactly to the dish (the number). 6's ingredients are 1+2+3=6 — the dish IS the ingredients. Your program is the chef searching for these magical recipes among all numbers.
try_it: Also find 'deficient' numbers (sum < n) and 'abundant' numbers (sum > n) in a range. Print counts of each. Try finding the 5th perfect number (33550336) — notice how much slower it gets. Why?
tips: Skip n itself when summing divisors — it's the 'proper' divisor condition
Check divisors only up to sqrt(n) — add both i and n/i in one go
All known perfect numbers are even — odd perfect numbers remain unproven
common_mistakes: Including n in the divisor sum — the sum must EXCLUDE n
Forgetting to add n/i as a divisor pair when checking up to sqrt
Double-counting perfect squares — 36's divisor 6 shouldn't be added twice
